source_text: Simili acumine illud quoque labefactare conaris, quod dixi, evangelico testimonio ex fructi bus suis arborem debere cognosci; ut ostenderem, quod clarum est, doceri bona non posse coniugia, immo ipsam naturam, quae coniugiorum operatione suppletur, nec Dei posse opere vindicari, si de ea dicerentur crimina pullulare. Ad hoc ergo respondisti: Numquid Dominus inde loquebatur, et non potius de duabus voluntatibus hominum, bona scilicet et mala; istam bonam, illam malam arborem dicens; quia de bona voluntate opera bona nascuntur, et mala de mala? Quod si nuptias arborem bonam intellegamus, profecto e contrario posituri sumus fornicationem arborem malam. Porro si dixerit non illic arboris loco ponendum esse adulterium, sed naturam humanam de qua nascitur homo ita et hic non erit arbor connubium, sed natura humana de qua nascitur homo [n44] . Falleris: non ibi Dominus loquitur de duabus voluntatibus, sed de persona sua. Quoniam cum beneficia Iudaeis praestaret innumera, ab eius nihil criminationibus desinebant. Ceterum cum opera eius, quae etiam glorificabant, arguere non valerent; ipsum tamen Samaritanum ac plenum daemonio et Behelzebulis spiritu causabantur illudere. Tunc ergo Dominus ait: Aut facite arborem bonam, et fructus eius bonos; aut facite arborem malam, et fructus eius malos: ex fructibus enim suis arbor dignoscitur [n45] . Id est: Aut opera mea vituperate, quae bona esse infirmitates pulsae et restitutae sanitates loquuntur; ut improbum me, operum meorum testimonio comprobetis; aut si haec tanta beneficia non audetis arguere; reddite bonae arbori, mihi videlicet, testimonium fructuum meorum, et amate beneficum, qui beneficia praedicatis. Ibi ergo personam de operibus suis Christus iussit agnosci; quod nobis iure suffragatum est, ut doceremus naturam quoque atque coniugia de fructificationis suae qualitate censenda; ut si de his criminum virus fluebat, criminosa etiam radix iudicaretur. Vide ergo quam ad intellegendum caecutias, qui levare te obiecti mei pondus putasti, fornicationem nuptiis ex adverso locando, ut sicut bona arbor nuptiae, ita mala fornicatio videretur, de qua, id est, fornicatione, fecunditas nulla deberet existere, ne mala convinceretur, si bonae nuptiae bonis fetibus probarentur; cum homo sive de coniugio, sive de adulterio nascitur, non de flagitio, sed de natura seminum prodeat. Flagitium quippe quod moechantium voluntate committitur, substantiae instituta non turbat; verum exercet se natura per materias suas, et peccato remanente apud illicitae voluntatis auctorem, fetus innocuus de opere Conditoris erumpit. Quod quidem et tu vidisti esse referendum; sed qualiter conatus sis eludere, prudens lector attendat. Ais enim: Si arboris loco ibi non est ponendum adulterium, sed natura humana de qua nascitur homo; ita et hic non erit arbor bona connubium, sed natura humana de qua nascitur homo. Hoc est ergo quod eloqui conatus es: Sicut non imputatur homo fornicationi, sed naturae; ita peccatum quod trahitur de parentibus legitimis, non esse imputandum connubio, sed naturae humanae, quam crimine diabolus infecit antiquo. In adulteris ergo culpasti lascivientium voluntatem, sed laudasti humanam naturam, de qua homo etiam per illicitos concubitus nasceretur; in parentibus autem legitimis laudasti connubium, de quo non dicis venire peccatum; sed vituperasti naturam, de qua dicis infundi crimen horrendum. Vigilet hic ergo lector meus. Si naturam humanam in fornicatione laudabilem censuisti, quae causam nascenti flagitiis coeuntium impollutam fecisset; quomodo hanc ipsam naturam in connubii parte reprehendis, quam dicis causam naturali crimini praestitisse? Ergo non quidem connubium, sed naturam humanam et magnum bonum et magnum malum esse professus es. Nam quid ea nequius, si crimen ingenuit? Quid detestabilius, si a diabolo possidetur? Quid ergo habeat artis in semine, ipsa viderit; qualitatis interim, in qua bonum omne vel malum est, pessimae comprobatur, si et ipsa rea, et generans reatus, et diabolicae convincitur tyrannidis satelles. Merito ergo de fructibus suis debet arbor agnosci, ut quae causa mali est, mala iure optimo nominetur.
pass_a_gloss: By a similar sharpness you try also to weaken that which I said, that by evangelical testimony a tree ought to be known from its fruits; that I might show, what is clear, that marriages cannot be taught good, nay nature itself, which is supplied by the operation of marriages, cannot even be claimed by God's work, if crimes were said to sprout from it. To this therefore you replied: Was the Lord speaking from there, and not rather about two wills of humans, namely good and evil; calling this the good tree, that the evil; because from a good will good works are born, and evil from an evil? Which if we understand marriages as a good tree, we will certainly from the contrary be about to place fornication as an evil tree. Further if he shall have said that adultery is not to be placed there in the place of a tree, but human nature from which a human is born, so also here the tree will not be wedlock, but human nature from which a human is born. You are deceived: the Lord does not speak there about two wills, but about his own person. Because when he was furnishing countless benefits to the Jews, they were not desisting from accusations of him. For the rest when they could not argue his works, which they were even glorifying; they themselves nevertheless were alleging that he, a Samaritan and full of a demon and of Beelzebul's spirit, was mocking. Then therefore the Lord said: Either make the tree good, and its fruits good; or make the tree evil, and its fruits evil: for from its fruits the tree is distinguished. That is: Either blame my works, which driven-out infirmities and restored healths speak to be good; that you may prove me wicked by the testimony of my works; or if you do not dare to accuse these so great benefits; render to the good tree, namely to me, the testimony of my fruits, and love the benefactor whose benefits you preach. There therefore Christ commanded a person to be recognized from his works; which has rightly suffraged us, that we might teach that nature also and marriages are to be judged from the quality of their fruiting; so that if the virus of charges was flowing from these, the root also would be judged criminal. See therefore how you are blind for understanding, you who thought to lift the weight of my objection by placing fornication opposite to marriages, so that as marriage is a good tree, so fornication would seem evil, from which, that is from fornication, no fertility ought to exist, lest it be convicted evil if good marriages were proved by good offspring; when a human, whether born from marriage or from adultery, comes forth not from outrage but from the nature of seeds. For the outrage which is committed by the will of adulterers does not disturb the institutions of substance; but nature exercises itself through its matters, and the sin remaining with the author of an illicit will, an innocent offspring bursts from the Founder's work. Which indeed you also saw must be reported; but how you tried to elude, let the prudent reader attend. For you say: If adultery is not to be placed there in the place of a tree, but human nature from which a human is born; so also here the good tree will not be wedlock, but human nature from which a human is born. This is therefore what you tried to utter: As a human is not imputed to fornication but to nature; so the sin which is drawn from legitimate parents is not to be imputed to wedlock, but to human nature, which the devil infected with an ancient charge. In adulterers therefore you blamed the will of the wanton, but praised human nature, from which a human would be born even through illicit couplings; but in legitimate parents you praised wedlock, from which you do not say sin comes; but you blamed nature, from which you say a horrible charge is poured. Let my reader therefore be watchful here. If you judged human nature praiseworthy in fornication, which had made an unpolluted cause for the one being born from the outrages of those coupling; how do you blame this same nature on the side of wedlock, which you say furnished a cause for a natural charge? Therefore you have professed that not indeed wedlock, but human nature is both a great good and a great evil. For what more worthless than it, if it generated a charge? What more detestable, if it is possessed by the devil? What art therefore it has in seed, let it itself see; of quality meanwhile, in which every good or evil is, it is proved of the worst, if it is convicted both itself guilty, and generating guilt, and a satellite of diabolical tyranny. Deservedly therefore a tree ought to be recognized from its fruits, so that what is a cause of evil may by best right be named evil.

pass_b_english: With similar sharpness you also try to undermine my use of the Gospel testimony that a tree must be known by its fruits. I used it to demonstrate the obvious: marriage cannot be shown good—nor, indeed, the nature replenished through marital activity—or vindicated as God’s work if crimes are said to sprout from it. You replied: ‘Was the Lord speaking about that, rather than about two human wills, the good and the evil? He called the former a good tree and the latter an evil tree, because good works arise from a good will and evil works from an evil one. If we understand marriage as a good tree, we must certainly place fornication opposite it as an evil tree. But if he says that adultery should not be put in the tree’s place there, but rather the human nature from which a human being is born, then here too the tree will not be marriage but the human nature from which a human being is born’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.26.43).

You are mistaken. The Lord is speaking there not about two wills but about his own person. Although he conferred countless benefits on the Jews, they never stopped accusing him. They could not condemn his works, which they even glorified; nevertheless they charged him with being a Samaritan, full of a demon, and deceiving them by Beelzebul’s spirit (John 8:48; Matthew 12:24). Then the Lord said: ‘Either make the tree good and its fruits good, or make the tree evil and its fruits evil; for a tree is recognized by its fruits’ (Matthew 12:33). That is: either criticize my works, whose goodness is attested by illnesses driven away and health restored, so that you establish my wickedness from the evidence of my works; or, if you do not dare condemn these great benefits, give the good tree—that is, me—the testimony of my fruits. You who praise the benefits must love the benefactor. There, then, Christ commanded that a person be recognized from his works. This rightly supported our teaching that nature and marriage too must be assessed from the quality of their fruitfulness. If the poison of crimes flowed from them, the root too should be judged criminal.

See how blind your understanding is. You thought you could lighten my objection’s weight by placing fornication opposite marriage, so that marriage would appear a good tree and fornication an evil one. Then no fertility should arise from fornication, lest it be proved evil if good marriage were proved by good offspring. But whether a human being is born from marriage or adultery, he proceeds not from shameful conduct but from the nature of seed. The shameful act committed by adulterers’ will does not disturb the arrangements of substance. Nature exercises itself through its own materials. The sin remains with the author of the unlawful will, while innocent offspring comes forth through the creator’s work. You too saw that this answer had to be given. But let the discerning reader attend to how you tried to evade it.

You say: ‘If adultery is not to be placed in the tree’s position there, but human nature from which a human being is born, then here too the good tree will not be marriage but human nature from which a human being is born.’ Here, then, is what you tried to express: just as a human being is not attributed to fornication but to nature, so the sin derived from lawful parents should not be attributed to marriage but to human nature, which the devil infected with an ancient crime. In adulterers, then, you blamed the wanton people’s will, but praised human nature, from which a human being was born even through unlawful intercourse. In lawful parents, however, you praised marriage, from which you deny sin comes, but criticized nature, from which you say a dreadful crime is poured forth.

Let my reader be alert here. If you judged human nature praiseworthy in fornication because it provided the newborn child’s origin unstained by the partners’ shameful acts, how do you condemn that same nature in marriage, saying it provided the cause of natural guilt? You have therefore professed not marriage but human nature to be both a great good and a great evil. What could be more wicked than it, if it engendered crime? What more detestable, if it is possessed by the devil? Let nature attend to whatever skill it has in seed. For the moment, in its quality—the sphere to which every good or evil belongs—it is proved utterly evil if it is itself guilty, produces guilt, and is convicted as the servant of diabolical tyranny. Rightly, then, a tree must be known by its fruits, so that what causes evil is most rightly called evil.

choices.why: Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
